title: The Thirst for Annihilation: Essex, Warwick, the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit, and the Shanghai Years
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Königsberg, the silent decade
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the silent decade is conventionally dated 1770-1781. The pin marks a span, not an event, and is inherited from kant.journey.json.
stops.campa: For eleven years Kant publishes almost nothing. Inside that silence the doctrine of time as the form of inner sense is worked out: the argument that time is not a thing found in the world but the shape the mind imposes before anything can be found at all. Two centuries later a doctoral student at Essex will make time the object of a thesis and be read, by some, as attacking exactly this. Land never comes here. The line runs by citation, not by road.
suggested_refs: The Transcendental Aesthetic of the Critique of Pure Reason, on time as the form of inner sense

stops.name: Königsberg, the Critique of Pure Reason
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1781; month and day not recorded and defaulted. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from kant.journey.json.
stops.campa: The book appears in 1781 and the Transcendental Aesthetic with it. One tradition holds that Land's Essex dissertation is called The Death of Time and takes that section as its direct object. Wikipedia says the dissertation is on Heidegger's essay about Georg Trakl's poetry. The two accounts describe different theses, no located source reconciles them, and neither is dropped here. Kant's book is the fixed point either way.
suggested_refs: Kant, Kritik der reinen Vernunft, first edition, Riga 1781
sources: kant.journey.json (stop 1781-01-01, 'Königsberg, the Critique of Pure Reason')
Wikipedia, 'Nick Land', Biography, for the Heidegger and Trakl thesis subject

stops.name: Tübingen, three students share a chamber
stops.date_confidence: attested to 18 October 1790; inherited from kant.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of October three young men are entered together in the Tübinger Stift: Hegel, Hölderlin, Schelling. Out of that shared chamber comes the post-Kantian line, idealism running from Kant through Hegel and onward. Land's doctorate positions itself against that line rather than inside it, a reading unconfirmed by any source located. He never goes to Swabia. He inherits the quarrel in translation and turns it toward Bataille, who is what German idealism looks like once the system is removed.
suggested_refs: The Tübinger Stift register for 1790, entering Hegel, Hölderlin and Schelling together
sources: kant.journey.json (stop 1790-10-18, 'Tübingen, three students share a chamber')

stops.name: Collège de France, Paris, the chair that grants no degree
stops.date_confidence: attested for each election: Lévi-Strauss 1959, Foucault 12 April 1970, Barthes 7 January 1977. The stop is dated to the earliest of the three; no month is recorded for it.
stops.campa: Lévi-Strauss takes his chair in 1959, Foucault in 1970, Barthes in 1977. The lectures are public and anyone may walk in off the street to hear them. Nobody enrols and nothing is conferred at the end. Thirty-six years after Lévi-Strauss's election, Land and Sadie Plant found a research unit at Warwick that runs the same machinery in reverse, inside a university, credentialed and hostile to the credential. None of the three chair-holders ever hears of the CCRU.
suggested_refs: The Collège de France inaugural lectures of Lévi-Strauss, Foucault and Barthes

stops.name: Johns Hopkins, Baltimore, the crossing
stops.date_confidence: attested to 18 October 1966; recorded identically in two existing corpus journeys.
stops.campa: The structuralism colloquium at Johns Hopkins gathers Derrida, Lacan, and a wave of French theorists before an American audience for the first time. It is the hinge at which French theory enters Anglophone academia and becomes, within a generation, something taught in English departments and philosophy faculties from Baltimore to Coventry. Land is four years old. The current that reaches Warwick in 1987, and is bent there into cybernetics and jungle records, passes through this room first.
suggested_refs: The Languages of Criticism and the Sciences of Man, Johns Hopkins, October 1966
sources: gilles_deleuze.journey.json and roland_barthes.journey.json, both stop 1966-10-18 'Johns Hopkins, Baltimore'

stops.name: Paris, the coordinate the corpus keeps returning to
stops.date_confidence: not an event: a shared default coordinate used across four corpus journeys for undated or unplaced Parisian stops, dated here to the year the Vincennes sequence opens.
stops.campa: Deleuze, Foucault, Barthes and Lévi-Strauss each pass dozens of undated years through this same stretch of Paris, a working address none of them fixed to a single door. Land has no Paris address in any record located. He orbits the coordinate by citation alone: every term he carries to Warwick, desiring-production, deterritorialization, the war machine, was written within a few kilometres of here. The intellectual hub is real. His physical presence at it is not, and is not claimed.
suggested_refs: The shared Paris default coordinate, 48.8566 / 2.3522, across four corpus journeys

stops.name: Vincennes, the philosophy department of Paris VIII
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1968; day not recorded and defaulted. Inherited from michel_foucault.journey.json.
stops.campa: Foucault builds a philosophy department in December, months after the barricades, on a site chosen for being nowhere in particular. Deleuze's weekly seminar runs here from 1971, open to anyone, transcribed by whoever brings a recorder. It is anti-disciplinary by construction: no syllabus that holds, no boundary between the enrolled and the curious. Twenty-seven years later Land and Sadie Plant assemble something with the same grammar in a university that had not asked for it. No source says they took Vincennes as a model.
suggested_refs: The founding of the Centre universitaire expérimental de Vincennes, December 1968

stops.name: Cour-Cheverny, the clinic at La Borde
stops.date_confidence: attested that Guattari's clinic is the milieu of the collaboration from 1970; month and day not recorded and defaulted. Inherited from gilles_deleuze.journey.json.
stops.campa: Guattari's psychiatric clinic in the Loir-et-Cher, where the roles of staff and patient are deliberately rotated so that nothing settles into hierarchy. Deleuze meets Guattari in Paris in 1969 and the collaboration begins here. The desiring-machine, the body without organs, the schizophrenic as a figure of production rather than deficit: all of it comes out of a working ward before it becomes a vocabulary. Land will take the vocabulary and strip the clinic out of it.
suggested_refs: La Borde clinic, Cour-Cheverny, and the practice of institutional psychotherapy

stops.name: Paris, rue Bernard-Palissy: Anti-Oedipus
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1972; day not recorded and defaulted. Coordinate inherited from gilles_deleuze.journey.json.
stops.campa: Éditions de Minuit publishes Capitalisme et schizophrénie, volume one. The book proposes that desire produces rather than lacks, that capital deterritorializes faster than any critique of it, and that psychoanalysis has been reading the wrong machine. Land's whole Warwick apparatus is built from these parts, reassembled with the brake removed: where Deleuze and Guattari describe a process, Land recommends it. The book travels; the authors, mostly, stay home.
suggested_refs: Deleuze and Guattari, L'Anti-Oedipe, Éditions de Minuit, 1972
sources: gilles_deleuze.journey.json (stop 1972-03-01, 'Editions de Minuit, rue Bernard-Palissy: Anti-Oedipus')

stops.name: Cerisy-la-Salle, Nietzsche aujourd'hui
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1972; day not recorded and defaulted. Inherited from gilles_deleuze.journey.json.
stops.campa: In a Normandy château in July the French read Nietzsche together for ten days: Deleuze, Lyotard, Derrida, Klossowski. The Nietzsche who comes out of the château is not the one German philology had kept. He is a Nietzsche of forces, intensities and expenditure, read through Bataille. Twenty years later Land's first book takes that reading to the point where the reader is told outright that it cannot be survived. Cerisy is the room where Nietzsche's afterlife turns French.
suggested_refs: The Cerisy-la-Salle colloquium Nietzsche aujourd'hui, July 1972, and its two published volumes

stops.name: Paris, rue Bernard-Palissy: A Thousand Plateaus
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1980; month and day not recorded and defaulted. Coordinate inherited from gilles_deleuze.journey.json.
stops.campa: Volume two, from the same publisher and the same street door. The war machine, nomadology, the smooth and the striated: terms that will recur throughout Land's Warwick essays and the CCRU's theory-fiction, usually with no source given and no sign that one is missing. Minuit prints it in Paris; Warwick reads it in translation. By 1980 Land is eighteen and no located source says where. The vocabulary he will spend a decade accelerating is finished and bound before he enters a university anyone can name.
suggested_refs: Deleuze and Guattari, Mille plateaux, Éditions de Minuit, 1980
sources: gilles_deleuze.journey.json (stop 1980-01-01, 'Editions de Minuit: A Thousand Plateaus')

stops.name: Pitié-Salpêtrière, Paris, two deaths at one address
stops.date_confidence: attested: Foucault 25 June 1984, Barthes 26 March 1980. The stop is dated to the later of the two and holds both.
stops.campa: Barthes dies in this hospital on the twenty-sixth of March 1980, a month after a laundry van struck him in the rue des Écoles. Foucault dies here on the twenty-fifth of June 1984. Their graves are elsewhere; the two deaths are some fifty metres apart on the map. The continental wing Land joins at Warwick three years afterward is by then missing its two most public figures. He arrives into a field whose founders are dying and writes as though that were not the point.
suggested_refs: The Pitié-Salpêtrière hospital, Paris, as a shared corpus pin for Barthes and Foucault

stops.name: England, the year 1962
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the Library of Congress name authority file, 'Land, Nick, 1962-'; month and day unknown and defaulted. Place unattested: no located source gives a country, town or day, and the coordinate is a placeholder England centroid, not a finding.
stops.campa: The Library of Congress name authority file records him as Land, Nick, 1962, and that is the whole of what is attested. Wikipedia's infobox carries the same year with a citation-needed tag beside it. No located source gives a country, a town, or a day. Web snippets circulate a Kent village and a March date; neither corroborates against anything citable and both are left out. The pin here stands in for a place no record names. The philosopher of the near-future begins this record without an address.
suggested_refs: Library of Congress name authority record, id.loc.gov, 'Land, Nick, 1962-'
sources: Library of Congress name authority file

stops.name: Wivenhoe Park, Colchester: the Essex doctorate
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1987; month and day not recorded and defaulted. Coordinate corrected to the University of Essex infobox value, 51.87633 N / 0.94487 E, replacing two conflicting and incorrect figures carried in the research pool.
stops.campa: He takes his PhD at Essex under David Farrell Krell, writing on Heidegger's 1953 essay Die Sprache im Gedicht, which reads the poetry of Georg Trakl. That is what Wikipedia records. Another tradition holds instead that the thesis is called The Death of Time and reads Kant's Transcendental Aesthetic. The two accounts describe different theses and nothing located reconciles them. Where he studied before Essex, no source says at all. The campus sits in a park at the edge of Colchester, built new in the 1960s.
suggested_refs: The Essex doctoral thesis of 1987, supervised by David Farrell Krell
sources: Wikipedia, 'University of Essex' infobox, for the coordinate

stops.name: University of Warwick, the lectureship
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1987; month and day not recorded and defaulted. Coordinate taken from the University of Warwick infobox and relabelled to the main campus: the research pool's 'Gibbet Hill' label was wrong, since Gibbet Hill houses Life Sciences and the pre-clinical medical school, not Philosophy.
stops.campa: The same year as the doctorate he is appointed lecturer in continental philosophy at Warwick, on a main campus that straddles the Coventry boundary into Warwickshire, and he holds the post eleven years. The philosophy department is small and unfashionable, and nobody above it is paying attention. Earlier accounts place him at Gibbet Hill, which is the satellite site for Life Sciences and the medical school; philosophy is not there. He spends the eleven years turning a lectureship into something the university cannot describe.
suggested_refs: The Warwick philosophy department of the late 1980s, Faculty of Social Sciences, main campus
sources: Wikipedia, 'University of Warwick' infobox, for the coordinate

stops.name: Manchester, a co-founder's doctorate
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1989; month and day not recorded and defaulted. This is Sadie Plant's stop and not Land's, included as context for the unit's second origin.
stops.campa: Sadie Plant takes her philosophy doctorate at Manchester, then moves through Birmingham to Warwick. She arrives carrying cyberfeminism, a reading of Irigaray crossed with weaving, telephony and the machine, and she brings the word cyber into a department that had been reading Bataille. This pin is hers and not his. It is set down because the unit they found together has two origins and only one of them is Land. By 1997 she will leave Warwick to write full-time and the unit will become entirely his.
suggested_refs: Sadie Plant, Zeros and Ones, and the cyberfeminist reading that reaches Warwick with her

stops.name: London, Routledge: The Thirst for Annihilation
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1992; month and day not recorded and defaulted. The pin is the publisher's city of record and not a place Land is shown to have travelled to; the imprint is London and New York.
stops.campa: Routledge publishes The Thirst for Annihilation: Georges Bataille and Virulent Nihilism, subtitled An Essay in Atheistic Religion, in London and New York at once. It is a book about Bataille that refuses to be a study of Bataille, written in a voice that has already stopped addressing examiners. It is often called his only monograph of the academic years. His own bibliography contradicts that, listing Machinic Postmodernism: Complexity, Technics and Regulation from SAGE in 1996. The address is pinned here; Land is in Coventry.
suggested_refs: Nick Land, The Thirst for Annihilation, Routledge, London and New York, 1992
sources: Library of Congress catalogue record for the 1992 Routledge edition

stops.name: Warwick, Machinic Desire
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no located source dates the essay. Wikipedia's 'Accelerationism' references it among undated CCRU-era texts. 1993 is a placement inside the Warwick period, not an attestation.
stops.campa: An essay appears in which Deleuze and Guattari are read through cyberpunk rather than through the clinic, and the desiring-machine stops being a figure for the unconscious and becomes a description of capital's hardware. Neither the date nor the venue is firmly recorded; secondary accounts place it in the Warwick years without a year. What the essay does is fixed even where its date is not. It turns a French vocabulary into a science-fiction one and makes the future, rather than the subject, the thing under analysis.
stops.quote: Metaphysics dissolves into psychotic cosmogony.
stops.quote_source: Robin Mackay and Ray Brassier, Editors' Introduction, in Nick Land, Fanged Noumena (Urbanomic/Sequence Press, 2011), p.2. The editors' words about Land, not Land's own.
suggested_refs: Nick Land, 'Machinic Desire', reprinted in Fanged Noumena
sources: Fanged Noumena, table of contents and Editors' Introduction

stops.name: Warwick, Meltdown
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1995 by the Fanged Noumena table of contents, correcting the widely repeated 1994; month and day not recorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: The text that will be quoted more than anything else he writes is composed at Warwick and dated 1995 in the Fanged Noumena contents, not 1994 as circulating accounts have it. It is not an argument. It is a countdown written in the present tense, punctuated by years that compress toward zero, and it treats the human species as a phase capital passes through on its way somewhere else. Read aloud it works as liturgy. Read as philosophy it makes a claim no department of the time was equipped to refuse.
stops.quote: The story goes like this: Earth is captured by a technocapital singularity as renaissance rationalization and oceanic navigation lock into commoditization take-off.
stops.quote_source: Nick Land, 'Meltdown' (1995), in Fanged Noumena: Collected Writings 1987-2007 (Urbanomic/Sequence Press, 2011), p.441, the essay's opening line
suggested_refs: Nick Land, 'Meltdown', in Fanged Noumena, pp.441-459
sources: Fanged Noumena, full OCR text, archive.org item 'fangednoumena', read directly

stops.name: Warwick, No Future
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1995 by the Fanged Noumena List of Sources, which calls it a previously unpublished conference paper of that year; month and day not recorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: A conference paper that is never published as a paper in his academic years, surfacing only in the 2011 collection, where the List of Sources dates it to 1995. Its subject is that the future has been used up: modernity manufactured the future as a product and the product has been discontinued. In the same pages Bataille is described as something a reader does not survive. No located source names the conference. The line arrives as a warning and reads, seven years later, as a description of what happens to the man who wrote it.
stops.quote: Modernity invented the future, but that's all over.
stops.quote_source: Nick Land, 'No Future' (1995), in Fanged Noumena, p.392
suggested_refs: Nick Land, 'No Future', a 1995 conference paper first printed in Fanged Noumena
sources: Fanged Noumena, List of Sources and full text, archive.org item 'fangednoumena'

stops.name: Paris, avenue Niel: a window in the same year
stops.date_confidence: attested to 4 November 1995; inherited from gilles_deleuze.journey.json. Its relation to the CCRU's founding is chronological coincidence only, flagged and not resolved.
stops.campa: Deleuze, unable to breathe, goes out of the window of his apartment at 84 avenue Niel on the fourth of November. Within weeks of that date, in a building outside Coventry, a research unit is being constituted whose entire working vocabulary is his. There is no causal link and none is claimed here; the two events share a calendar year and nothing else, noted because the coincidence deserves a reader's attention and not an argument.
suggested_refs: 84 avenue Niel, Paris, 4 November 1995

stops.name: Warwick, the unit is founded
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia gives 'late 1995' for the formal establishment; December is the compiler's placement inside that phrase and not an attested month. The same article records Sadie Plant running a cyberfeminist research group at Warwick from 1993-94, and the two accounts are not reconciled by any located source.
stops.campa: Land and Sadie Plant constitute the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit inside the philosophy department. Graham Harman later describes what it welds together: futurism, technoscience, mysticism, numerology, complexity theory, science fiction. It produces hyperstition, the practice of writing fictions engineered to make themselves true, and the Numogram, a numerological machine for sorting time. Its output goes into zines rather than journals, among them the lowercase collapse, edited by Robin Mackay from 1995.
stops.quote: Meltdown: planetary china-syndrome, dissolution of the biosphere into the technosphere, terminal speculative bubble crisis, ultravirus, and revolution stripped of all christian-socialist eschatology (down to its burn-core of crashed security).
stops.quote_source: Nick Land, 'Meltdown' (1995), in Fanged Noumena, p.442. In the book the sentence follows the section head '[[ ]] Beyond the Judgment of God.'
suggested_refs: The zine collapse (lowercase), Warwick 1995-1996, ed. Robin Mackay with Robert O'Toole, distinct from Urbanomic's later Collapse journal

stops.name: Warwick, hyperstition: the fiction that makes itself real
stops.date_confidence: interpretive as to date. Hyperstition is a coinage of the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit circle in the late 1990s and is not attested to a single dated text in any source consulted; the term is most visible later, in the Hyperstition weblog of the mid-2000s. The date here is an ordering device inside the unit's Warwick years. The reading against Austin and Searle is this atlas's own: Land is nowhere on record deriving hyperstition from speech act theory, and the relation is one of apparatus, not of influence. Coordinate inherited from this file's own Warwick pin.
stops.campa: The unit's coinage for a fiction that makes itself real. Austin named the class of utterance that does not describe but does, and hedged it with felicity conditions: the right mouth, the right office, an institution behind the words. Searle hardened the hedge into a rule, X counts as Y in context C, holding only while enough people accept it. Hyperstition is that operation with the licence torn out. A prophecy stays open until someone is fitted to it, and the fitting is the whole event: the sentence was not true, and is true afterwards. Nothing authorises the fitting. It runs on circulation, and it works.
suggested_refs: j_l_austin.journey.json, 'Oxford, the course called Words and Deeds', where the performative is set out
john_searle.journey.json, 'Berkeley: the declaration, and the word that makes it so', on the constitutive rule a hyperstition does without

stops.name: Warwick Arts Centre, Virtual Futures 96
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1996; the month of the session is not recorded in the located sources and is defaulted. Coordinate corrected to the Warwick Arts Centre infobox value, 52.3798 N / 1.5617 W, replacing a pool figure some 150 metres off.
stops.campa: The conference series advertises itself as an anti-disciplinary event and as a conference in the post-humanities, two phrases quoted separately in the sources and kept separate here. At the 1996 session Land does not read a paper. Robin Mackay remembers him lying on the ground croaking into a microphone while Mackay played jungle records over him. It is the point at which the difference between a philosophy seminar and a rave stops being a distinction the university can enforce on its own premises.
stops.quote: Nothing human makes it out of the near-future.
stops.quote_source: Nick Land, 'Meltdown' (1995), in Fanged Noumena, p.443
suggested_refs: Virtual Futures 96, Warwick Arts Centre, and Robin Mackay's recollection of the session
sources: Wikipedia, 'Warwick Arts Centre' infobox, for the coordinate

stops.name: Warwick, Sadie Plant leaves
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1997; month and day not recorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: Plant resigns her post to write full-time and the unit's second origin walks out of it. What is left is Land, a set of graduate students, and no institutional brake. The cyberfeminist half of the founding programme thins; the accelerationist half does not. Kodwo Eshun, Mark Fisher, Ray Brassier, Reza Negarestani and Steve Goodman pass through the milieu across its life. The department that houses the unit has, by this point, very little idea what it is housing or under whose name.
suggested_refs: Sadie Plant's departure from Warwick, 1997, and the CCRU's roster of affiliates

stops.name: Warwick, CyberGothic and the resignation
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1998 for both the essay and the resignation; months not recorded and defaulted. No located source dates one relative to the other.
stops.campa: In the same year that he writes CyberGothic he resigns the lectureship. Eleven years after his appointment he leaves with no other post to go to, and the unit goes with him: it is not disbanded, it is simply no longer anywhere the university can point at. Nothing in the located sources says he was pushed and nothing says he was not. What he had spent a decade describing as a process with the brake off now happens to his own career. The building stays. The seminar moves to a flat.
stops.quote: Cybergothic is an affirmative telecommercial dystopianism, guided by schizoanalysis in marking actuality as primary repression, or collapsed potential, foot down hard on the accelerator.
stops.quote_source: Nick Land, 'CyberGothic' (1998), in Fanged Noumena, p.350
suggested_refs: Nick Land, 'CyberGothic', 1998, reprinted in Fanged Noumena
sources: Fanged Noumena, full text, archive.org item 'fangednoumena'

stops.name: Warwick town, a toponym the corpus already holds
stops.date_confidence: not an event: a note distinguishing two sites that share a name, dated to the year Land leaves the university. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from tolkien.journey.json, the St Mary Immaculate stop.
stops.campa: The name is a false friend on the map: the medieval county town of Warwick, with its castle and its market square, is not where the University of Warwick stands. The campus lies some ten kilometres north, outside Coventry, and takes the county's name without taking the county town, a piece of naming that has confused visitors since the university opened in 1965. Between the old town and the new campus runs a stretch of Warwickshire in which, within a year, an exiled research unit will be meeting in somebody's front room.
suggested_refs: St Mary Immaculate, Warwick, and the University of Warwick campus, two sites under one name
sources: tolkien.journey.json (stop, 'St Mary Immaculate, Warwick, the marriage')

stops.name: Warwick, Flatline Constructs
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1999; month and day not recorded and defaulted.
stops.campa: Mark Fisher completes his doctorate at Warwick, Flatline Constructs: Gothic Materialism and Cybernetic Theory-Fiction, written inside the milieu Land had led and finished after Land has gone. It is the CCRU's argument submitted, formatted and passed. Fisher will spend the next two decades taking the same materials in the opposite political direction, and in 2011 he will write the article that reintroduces Land to a reading public. The student outlives the unit; the teacher does not outlive the decade in public.
suggested_refs: Mark Fisher, Flatline Constructs, University of Warwick doctoral thesis, 1999

stops.name: Leamington Spa, a flat and no year
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source gives a year for the move. Wikipedia says only that the CCRU continued to operate from a flat in Leamington Spa up until Land's breakdown in the early 2000s. The range runs from the 1998 resignation to that breakdown, and 1999 is a placement inside it.
stops.campa: The unit keeps meeting after its founder has no employer, in a flat in Leamington Spa, unaffiliated with any university and answerable to nobody. Wikipedia gives no date for the move, only that the CCRU continued operating there up until Land's breakdown and disappearance in the early 2000s. So the flat is bounded on one side by the 1998 resignation and on the other by a collapse whose year no source states. It is the last address at which the thing begun in a philosophy department is still assembling.
stops.quote: was never formally disbanded but then again it was never formally constituted
stops.quote_source: Mark Fisher on the CCRU, quoted via Wikipedia, 'Cybernetic Culture Research Unit'
suggested_refs: The Leamington Spa flat, last operating address of the CCRU

stops.name: A place no source names, the breakdown
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Wikipedia says only 'in the early 2000s'. No located source gives 2001 or any specific year, and none names a location; the date is a placement inside the stated range and the coordinate repeats the last known address for want of any other.
stops.campa: After what Wikipedia calls a period of fanatical amphetamine abuse, he suffers a breakdown and disappears from public view. The unit dissolves around the same time. No located source names a year, a clinic, a town, or a witness, and the pin sits at the last known address because there is nowhere else to put it. For most of a decade the most cited unpublished philosopher in Britain is simply not anywhere. What he had written about acceleration and the brake now reads, from outside, as a note left in advance.
stops.quote: Bataille incinerates the soul, and is impossible to endure. You either die or go somewhere else. Or both.
stops.quote_source: Nick Land, 'No Future' (1995), in Fanged Noumena, p.391
suggested_refs: The early-2000s disappearance, dated by every located source only to a range

stops.name: Shanghai, an arrival with no date
stops.date_confidence: contested. Wikipedia's residency marker is 2017 and the Guardian confirms residence in May of that year, but Land publishes two Shanghai guidebooks in 2010. The date here follows the earlier evidence; the arrival itself is undated in every located source, and the contradiction is not resolved.
stops.campa: He resurfaces in Shanghai. Wikipedia states only that as of 2017 he resided there, and the Guardian confirms it in May of that year. But his own bibliography holds two Shanghai guidebooks published in 2010, and a man does not write a city's Expo guide from abroad. The two readings are not reconciled by any located source and are left standing side by side. Somewhere between the Leamington flat and Pudong there is a crossing no record holds: no visa, no year, no port of entry, no arrival.
stops.quote: Neo-China arrives from the future.
stops.quote_source: Nick Land, 'Meltdown' (1995), in Fanged Noumena, p.442
suggested_refs: Shanghai Basics, China Intercontinental Press, 2010, one of two Shanghai guidebooks in Land's bibliography

stops.name: Expo Axis, Pudong: the World Expo guide
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2010; the stop is dated to the Expo's opening on 1 May 2010 and not to any recorded action by Land. Coordinate corrected to the Expo Axis infobox value, 31.185733 N / 121.487986 E; the pool's figure was the Expo site centroid under an Expo Axis label.
stops.campa: Expo 2010 runs from the first of May to the thirty-first of October across the Huangpu, and China Intercontinental Press publishes The Shanghai World Expo Guide 2010 with his name on it. The Expo Axis is the covered spine of the site, a kilometre of glazed canopy funnelling seventy million visitors past the pavilions. The authorship is attested; whether he ever walked the Axis is not. The man who wrote that nothing human makes it out of the near-future is writing visitor copy for the largest world's fair yet staged.
suggested_refs: The Shanghai World Expo Guide 2010, China Intercontinental Press
sources: Wikipedia, 'Expo Axis' infobox, for the coordinate

stops.name: Falmouth, Urbanomic: Fanged Noumena
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2011; month and day not recorded and defaulted. The pin is the press's address of record and not a place Land is shown to have visited.

stops.campa: The city closes. stops.name: Warwick, the ten zones and their currents
stops.date_confidence: the numogram material is undated in the unit's own papers, which are collected only in 2015 as Ccru, Writings 1997-2003; no located source dates the diagram to a month or a year. The date is an ordering device inside the unit's Warwick life. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from this file's own Warwick pin.
stops.campa: Ten zones, numbered nought to nine, pair off by the sums that make nine: nine with nought, eight with one, seven with two. Each pair is a syzygy, and the difference inside a pair is a current running to a tractor zone. Add a zone's digits and the sum names a gate; reduce the gate and the reduction sets a channel, and the channels are the diagram's time-holes. It is arithmetic, used as a map of time. The three middle currents close into a rotating loop the unit calls the Time-Circuit. The upper and lower currents fold back on themselves, into what the papers call Outer-time.

stops.name: Warwick, the book nobody wrote
stops.date_confidence: interpretive, and dated only to order the segment. Lovecraft dies in 1937, twenty-five years before Land is born; this is Land's own apparatus applied backward to an object he did not treat in any located text, the same move licensed for Austin and Searle and recorded in EXCEPTIONS.md. Coordinate inherited from this file's own Warwick pin. Land is nowhere on record making this argument about the Necronomicon in these words.
stops.campa: Lovecraft invents a book, gives it a dead Arab author and a chain of translations, and quotes it in stories he sells to a pulp magazine. He never writes it. Libraries afterwards receive requests for it, forgers supply editions, and a title with no text acquires a bibliography. Land's own term names exactly this operation: a fiction that makes itself real by circulating, needing no authority and no author, only enough hands. Austin demanded the right mouth and the right office before a form of words could do anything. The Necronomicon has neither, was uttered by nobody, and is on the shelves.
stops.quote: Graham Harman also cited Land as the first philosopher in recent times to seriously engage with Lovecraft.
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Nick Land', reporting Harman's judgement. The sentence is Wikipedia's, the claim is Harman's, and neither is Land's own.

stops.campa: He serialises a book about Bitcoin on his own blog, version 1.0 dated the last day of October. The argument is that the currency is a critique of trusted third parties, and that this is critique in the strict Kantian sense: not an objection but an inquiry into what a system can do without. Kant asked what the understanding may do with no appeal to experience. Land asks what a ledger may do with no appeal to a bank. The line runs back to Königsberg, and it is Land who draws it, in his own sentence, not a reader drawing it for him.

stops.campa: He goes on a podcast and explains the diagram out loud, decades after it was drawn: the two sides of the Barker spiral, Atlantean and Lemurian; digital reduction; the triangular numbers; the Tetractys; the I Ching; the outside. No transcript has been located and this account rests on the episode's show notes, which is a weaker footing than any other stop here. What is certain is that a thing built as theory-fiction inside a philosophy department is now walked through by its author in the ordinary voice of a man on a call.

stops.name: Shanghai, Christ dressed up as a computer
stops.date_confidence: the episode date is not stated in any located source. A Substack recap dated 26 March 2026 reports the exchange, and Greer's own account of a two-and-a-half-hour call belongs to roughly the same month; the date follows the recap. Land's reply is quoted through that recap and not from audio, so it is reported at one remove.
stops.campa: On the same podcast an occultist tells him what the Singularity is: American Protestant Christian fundamentalism under a very thin layer of technological drag, the second coming with Christ dressed up as a computer. Land does not object. He answers that this is probably what he is doing too. In the same period he tells another interviewer that there are not two things going on, Silicon Valley building superintelligence on one side and a spiritual realm full of demonic entities on the other, and calls the present an eschatological moment of triumphant liberal technology.
stops.quote: That's probably what I'm doing, too.
stops.quote_source: Nick Land, replying to John Michael Greer on The Dangerous Maybe, quoted in a recap published on the Substack theflynneffect, 26 March 2026. Greer's preceding line: 'The whole singularity thing in his presentation is basically just the second coming of Christ except Christ is dressed up as a computer.'
